title: What a forecast really promises
logline: A probability is a frequency, not a verdict — judge forecasts by calibration and plan for the misses.
audience: Professionals who read forecasts but never learned to read probability.

music.prompt: Minimal modern ambient, soft felt piano, warm pads, very light pulse

beats.vo: Seventy percent. <short pause> Is that a promise?

props.label: chance the launch ships on time

beats.vo: A probability isn't a verdict. It's how often you should expect to be surprised.

props.text: A probability isn't a verdict. It's how often you should expect to be *surprised*.

beats.vo: Picture a hundred launches with that forecast. About seventy ship on time. About thirty slip.
The word for a trustworthy forecaster is calibrated: of everything they call seventy percent, about seventy percent happens.

props.definition: Of a forecaster: events they call 70% happen about 70% of the time.

beats.vo: So write the forecast down, check it against what happened, and adjust.
And stop asking whether a forecast was right. Ask whether you planned for the thirty.
